mainTopic: The order of ירושה among son, father and brothers, and the דרשה of 'שארו' and 'הקרוב'
overview: The גמרא finishes asking why our משנה opens with a father inheriting his son, when the פסוק itself first mentions a son inheriting. It answers that the תנא loved the father's ירושה because it is learned only through a דרשה. The גמרא then quotes that ברייתא. 'שארו' teaches that the father comes before the dead man's brothers, and 'הקרוב' teaches that whoever is closer comes first, so the son comes before the father. The ברייתא asks why the son, and not the brother, is the closer one. The son stands in his father's place for יעוד and for a שדה אחוזה. When the ברייתא counters that the brother stands in his brother's place for יבום, it answers that יבום only happens when there is no son. The amud ends with the גמרא asking why that argument was needed at all, since the son's priority could be learned from another source. That question continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The verse itself puts the son first
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא adds a second reason the משנה should have listed the son inheriting the father first: the פסוק about ירושה opens with the son.
steps.simpleTranslation: And furthermore, as it is written: 'If a man dies and has no son.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing its question on the משנה's order by adding one more point. The תורה's ירושה section starts with the son.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה began with a father inheriting his son. The גמרא says this seems backwards, because the פסוק first assumes a son inherits ('and has no son'), and only after that lists other relatives. So the son inheriting should be the opening case.

keyTerms.meaning: And furthermore: adding another point to an argument already started
As it is written (in a פסוק)
And he has no son

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new question. It is the second half of a question that began just before, about why the משנה starts with the father.

phrases.english: And furthermore, as it is written:
"If a man dies and has no son"

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues a question on the משנה's order that began before this section
steps.kashyaTarget: The order of cases in the משנה (father inheriting son listed first)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק presents the son's ירושה first, so the משנה should follow that order.

steps.title: The תנא loved the law that comes from a דרשה
steps.stepSummary: The תנא listed the father first because the father's ירושה is learned only through a דרשה, which made it dear to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the תנא: since this law comes to him from a derivation, it is dear to him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. The תנא put the father first because that law comes from a דרשה and not from an open פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A son inheriting is written plainly in the תורה, but a father inheriting has to be drawn out by careful reading. A law that took effort to learn was especially beloved, so the תנא gave it first place. The order says nothing about which relative is closer.

keyTerms.meaning: The teacher of the משנה or ברייתא
Since, because
A law derived from close reading of a פסוק
It is dear (beloved) to him

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a common way the גמרא explains a משנה's order: a law learned through a דרשה may be listed first because it was beloved, not because it is more basic.

phrases.english: And the tanna: since it comes to him
phrases.notes: 'It' means the law that a father inherits his son.

phrases.english: from a derivation, it is dear to him!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the משנה's order
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the order by the תנא's affection for a law learned from a דרשה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה's order should follow the פסוק and how basic each case is.
steps.terutzMaskana: The תנא chose to open with the law learned through a דרשה, because it was dear to him.

steps.title: Asking which derivation this is
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the דרשה is that teaches a father inherits his son.
steps.whatsHappening: This short question sets up the next step. The גמרא wants to see the actual source for the father's ירושה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer in step 2 rests on the claim that the father's ירושה comes from a דרשה. So the גמרא now asks to see that דרשה.

keyTerms.meaning: And what?

phrases.english: And what is the derivation?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source behind the claim made in the answer
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The דרשה that teaches a father inherits his son

steps.title: His kinsman is the father, and closer comes first
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא reads 'שארו' as the father, who comes before the brothers. It reads 'הקרוב' as teaching that the closer relative inherits first, so the son comes before the father.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is taught in a ברייתא: 'His kinsman' means the father. This teaches that the father comes before the brothers. You might think he also comes before the son. So the פסוק says 'the one closest': whoever is closer comes first.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a ברייתא. Two words in the פסוק set the father's place: after the son, before the brothers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'שארו' (his kinsman) is read as the father, which puts him ahead of the dead man's brothers. Someone might then think the father beats even the son. The word 'הקרוב' (the closest) teaches that closeness decides the order, and the son counts as closer than the father.

keyTerms.meaning: His kinsman (his own flesh); read here as the father
This teaches
One might have thought
Therefore the פסוק says (to teach otherwise)
The one closest (in relation)

steps.whatToRemember: Order so far: son first, then father, then the dead man's brothers. 'שארו' puts the father ahead of the brothers, and 'הקרוב' keeps the son ahead of the father.

phrases.english: As it is taught: "His kinsman" — this is the father;
this teaches that the father comes before the brothers.
One might think he should come before the son?
Therefore the verse says: "The one closest" —
whoever is closer comes first.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the request for the דרשה
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'שארו' is the father, who comes before the brothers. 'הקרוב' teaches that the closer relative comes first, so the son comes before the father.

steps.title: Why count the son as closer, and not the brother?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks why we treat the son as closer than the father, instead of treating the brother as closer.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what did you see to include the son and to exclude the brother?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא challenges its own reading. Why use 'הקרוב' to put the son ahead of the father, and not to put the brother ahead of him?
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'הקרוב' tells us someone is closer than the father, but it does not say who. The son and the brother are both possible. The ברייתא needs a reason to pick the son, which leaves the brother still after the father.

keyTerms.meaning: What did you see (what is your reason)
To include
To exclude

phrases.english: And what did you see to include the son,
phrases.notes: Include him as the 'closer' relative who comes before the father.

phrases.english: and to exclude the brother?

steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the son, and not the brother, is the relative 'closer' than the father

steps.title: The son stands in his father's place
steps.stepSummary: The son is chosen because he takes his father's place in two laws: יעוד of an אמה עבריה and redeeming a שדה אחוזה.
steps.simpleTranslation: I include the son, since he stands in place of his father for designation, and for an ancestral field.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers that the son is the closer one. He legally steps into his father's shoes in two areas, and a brother does not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In two הלכות the תורה treats a son as continuing his father. He can do יעוד, marrying the אמה עבריה his father bought. If he redeems a שדה אחוזה his father made הקדש, the field returns at יובל as if the father redeemed it. Since the son already acts as his father's stand-in, he counts as 'closer' than the father, ahead of the brother.

keyTerms.meaning: I include
Stands in place of his father
Designating an אמה עבריה as a wife
An inherited family field

steps.whatToRemember: Order from this ברייתא: son, then father, then brothers. The son is chosen because he 'stands in place of his father' for יעוד and for a שדה אחוזה. The next step challenges this.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the halachic order of ירושה: a dead man's son comes before his father, and his father comes before his brothers.

phrases.english: I include the son —
since he stands in place of his father
for designation and for an ancestral field.
phrases.notes: So the son can marry his father's אמה עבריה, and if he redeems his father's הקדש field, it goes back to the family at יובל.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers why the son is the closer relative
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The son takes his father's place for יעוד and for a שדה אחוזה, so he is closer than the father, and the brother is not.

steps.title: Maybe the brother should be the closer relative
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא argues the reverse: the brother should be included as 'closer', because he takes his dead brother's place for יבום.
steps.simpleTranslation: On the contrary! I should include the brother, since he stands in his brother's place for יבום!
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא pushes back on its own answer from Step 6. It says the brother also takes the dead man's place, in the law of יבום, so maybe he should be the 'closer' one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 6 the son won because he steps into his father's shoes in two laws. Now the ברייתא uses the same kind of reasoning for the brother. The brother steps into his dead brother's shoes in יבום, so the comparison now looks even.

keyTerms.meaning: On the contrary; the opposite is true
I include (in the word הקרוב, 'the closer one')
Stands in the place of; takes over for
Levirate marriage: a brother marries his dead brother's childless widow

phrases.english: On the contrary!
I should include the brother,
phrases.notes: Include him as the 'closer' relative learned from the word הקרוב in Step 4.

phrases.english: since he stands in his brother's place for levirate marriage!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Counters Step 6's reason with a matching reason in favor of the brother.
steps.kashyaTarget: Step 6's claim that the son is closer because he takes his father's place.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If taking someone's place makes you closer, the brother also takes his brother's place in יבום, so he could be the closer one.

steps.title: יבום only happens when there is no son
steps.stepSummary: The brother's role in יבום proves nothing, because יבום only exists when there is no son. Even there, the son comes first.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is there any יבום except where there is no son? Where there is a son, there is no יבום.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers the push-back. A brother only does יבום when the dead man left no son, so the son still ranks ahead of the brother.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The brother's 'taking over' depends on the son not being there. That shows the son outranks the brother even in the brother's own law. So the son stays the 'closer' relative.

keyTerms.meaning: Is there anything at all…? (a rhetorical question)
In a case where there is no son

steps.whatToRemember: The son comes before the father and before the brother. The brother's יבום only applies when there is no son.

phrases.english: Is there any levirate marriage
except in a case where there is no son?

phrases.aramaic: הָא בְּמָקוֹם שֶׁיֵּשׁ בֵּן – אֵין יִבּוּם.
phrases.english: But in a case where there is a son, there is no levirate marriage.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּלוּם יֵשׁ יִבּוּם אֶלָּא בְּמָקוֹם שֶׁאֵין בֵּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 7 by showing that the brother's role depends on there being no son.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Turns the challenger's own proof around: the law of יבום itself shows the son outranks the brother.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The brother takes his brother's place in יבום, so he might be the closer relative.
steps.terutzMaskana: יבום only happens when there is no son, so the son stays ahead of the brother.

steps.title: Why was this argument even needed?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that the ברייתא needed the יבום argument to rank the son over the brother. It starts to ask why we don't learn this from another source.
steps.simpleTranslation: The reason is only because of this answer. Without it, would I have said the brother is stronger? Let him learn it from…
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now looks back at the ברייתא and questions it. This line sets up a challenge, and the sentence continues on the next amud, where the other source is named.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא used the יבום argument to keep the son ahead of the brother. That suggests that without it, the brother could have won. The גמרא finds this odd, because the son's priority over the brother should be clear from somewhere else.

keyTerms.meaning: The reason is (only) because…
A refutation; an argument that knocks down a claim
I would have said (a first impression that later turns out wrong)
Better; ranks higher
Let him derive it from…; why not learn it from another source?

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new speaker inside the ברייתא. The גמרא itself is now questioning the ברייתא's line of reasoning.

phrases.english: The reason is because there is this refutation,
phrases.notes: This is the answer from Step 8: where there is a son, there is no יבום.

phrases.english: but if not for this,
would I have said that a brother is superior?
Let him derive it
phrases.notes: The sentence keeps going on the next amud, where the גמרא names the source.

steps.triggerLanguage: טַעְמָא דְּאִיכָּא הַאי פִּירְכָא, הָא לָאו הָכִי הֲוָה אָמֵינָא אָח עֲדִיף? תִּיפּוֹק לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws an implication from Steps 7–8 and begins challenging the need for that argument.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's reliance on the יבום argument to place the son ahead of the brother.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Relying on this argument implies that without it the brother could outrank the son. The גמרא thinks the son's priority can be learned from another source.
